_comment: THE DESIGN THEMES, for BOTH halves of the generator.
This file is the single source of truth. catalog_processor/app/themes.py reads it to
build the image prompts and to find each theme's reference photographs;
backend/src/services/themes.service.ts reads it so the step that PICKS the tiles is
held to the same specification. Node and Python run as separate functions on Vercel
with no shared disk and no shared package, so they cannot import one module -- but
they can read one file, and vercel.json bundles it into both.
Keys are normalised labels: lower case, separators collapsed, '&' spelled out. The
wizard sends the label (frontend/mood-board.html, THEMES) and both readers normalise
it the same way, so 'Roman Touch', 'ROMAN_TOUCH' and 'roman-touch' are one theme.
`slug` names the folder under catalog_processor/assets/theme_references/. A theme with
no folder has no references, which the prompt states outright rather than implying.
`mandatory` and `avoid` are the catalog owner's own rules and prohibitions. They are
sent to the model in full. Do not summarise them into a colour list: a theme reduced
to its palette is how eight themes come back as one generic bathroom.
`rooms` is optional, and keyed by the room's own noun in client_selections.py SPACES.
A theme's description is written once for every space it can be asked for; an entry
here says what that theme's furnishing looks like in ONE of them -- the sofas and the
coffee table of a floral living room, which have no meaning in a floral bathroom. It
is appended under IN THIS ROOM, and a theme with no entry for the selected room says
nothing extra, exactly as before.

british.label: British
british.palette: Heritage green, oxblood/burgundy, warm ivory, antique brass
british.identity: An authentic British Heritage / Victorian English country-house bathroom. The ARCHITECTURE carries it, not the accessories: deep forest and heritage green wall treatments, oxblood and burgundy accents, warm ivory and cream wall panelling, antique brass fixtures and hardware, Victorian or Edwardian architectural detailing, traditional framed mirrors and decorative mouldings, classic British panelled vanity cabinetry, heritage-inspired patterned flooring, traditional sanitaryware and a freestanding bathtub where the room suits one, and elegant botanical or heritage wallpaper as a CONTROLLED accent. A modern bathroom wearing a few British-inspired accessories is not this theme.
mandatory: The flooring must be traditional British patterned work -- Victorian encaustic-style pattern or a subtle heritage geometric motif -- in a coordinated ivory, dark green, burgundy and muted neutral palette. Plain undifferentiated flooring is not enough.
The walls must carry Victorian panelling, wainscoting and decorative mouldings, balanced against heritage-green surfaces.
The vanity must be traditional British cabinetry: detailed panelled fronts, classic proportions, antique brass handles, refined detailing.
Taps, shower fittings, towel rails and sanitaryware must be coordinated antique or aged brass and traditional in form.
Victorian or Edwardian character must be carried by architecture -- decorative mirror frames, cornices, panelling, traditional proportions -- not by ornaments placed in the room.
Botanical or heritage wallpaper is a CONTROLLED accent. It must not cover the shower area or dominate the room; balance it against traditional British tile or stone surfaces.
Green and/or oxblood must be meaningfully represented where the selected catalog tiles and the references allow it.

Blue feature walls and sage-grey subway tiles must NOT dominate the composition unless they are the actual selected catalog products. Where they are, keep them and build the heritage character around them with panelling, cabinetry, brass, mirrors and flooring.
Grey or blue surfaces may appear where the actual catalog products or the references require them, but must not turn the room into a generic contemporary bathroom.
A burgundy vanity and brass taps alone do not establish the theme.
avoid: oversized botanical wallpaper covering every surface or the whole shower area
modern floating vanities without heritage character
random decorative accessories with no architectural purpose
a contemporary subway-tile bathroom carrying only a burgundy vanity and brass fixtures
a modern bathroom with a few British-inspired accessories standing in for the style
british.success: The complete room reads as a British heritage or English country-house bathroom before any individual accessory is examined -- from its panelling, cabinetry, flooring and architectural detailing together, not from the vanity colour and the taps.
visible: The British heritage identity is immediately recognisable.
Victorian or Edwardian architectural detailing is visible -- panelling, wainscoting, cornices or decorative mouldings.
Heritage green and/or oxblood are meaningfully represented.
Traditional panelled cabinetry, a classic framed mirror and traditional brass fittings are present.
The flooring is traditional patterned work that supports the heritage aesthetic, not plain undifferentiated floor.
Botanical detailing is balanced and controlled rather than dominating a wall or the shower.
The complete room looks like a professionally designed British country-house bathroom, not a generic modern interior.
counts: Forest-green or heritage-green CABINETRY counts as heritage green. It does not have to be on the walls.
A burgundy or oxblood BATHTUB, vanity or textile counts toward the oxblood palette.
A Victorian-style or ornate framed MIRROR counts as heritage architectural detailing.
Traditional PANELLED cabinetry counts as British-inspired styling and as architectural detailing.
Antique or aged BRASS fixtures count as heritage hardware.
Patterned, encaustic, mosaic or bordered FLOORING counts as heritage-inspired flooring.
Large-format stone-effect or marble-effect wall tiles are NOT subway tiles and are NOT contemporary styling on their own. A heritage room may legitimately use large stone panels.
Botanical detailing is optional. Mark it missing only if the room plainly needed it and has none; a coherent British room without botanical pattern is not a failure.

roman touch.label: Roman Touch
roman touch.palette: Travertine, warm limestone, sand, beige, muted terracotta
roman touch.identity: A Roman-inspired architectural bathing space with a strong natural-stone identity. Warm travertine or limestone textures, substantial stone surfaces, arched niches, sculptural stone basins, restrained terracotta accents and soft architectural lighting. It should feel like a refined Mediterranean bathhouse, or a contemporary reading of classical Roman architecture. Stone, arches, mass, proportion and natural materials come first.
mandatory: Natural stone must be a major visual component.
Arches, recessed niches, sculptural forms or other convincing architectural details must communicate classical influence.
Terracotta stays an accent; it must not turn the design into a rustic clay bathroom.
Surfaces should feel substantial, warm and architectural.
Never present a selected catalog tile as travertine if it is a different material.
avoid: tropical greenery as the dominant theme
roman touch.success: The bathroom reads as Roman-inspired stone architecture or a Mediterranean bathhouse, not an ordinary bathroom with beige tiles.
visible: Natural stone is a major visual component of the room.
Arches, recessed niches or sculptural stone forms communicate classical influence.
Surfaces read as substantial, warm and architectural.
Terracotta is present as an accent rather than as the dominant material.

floral.label: Floral
floral.palette: Blush pink, sage green, ivory, soft botanical tones
floral.identity: A room where botanical design is a defining part of the interior. Flower-patterned tiles, botanical wall treatments, floral feature surfaces or other clearly visible floral elements, following the supplied references. The pattern is a CONTROLLED feature: ONE dominant floral surface, with the walls around it plain blush, ivory or sage so the pattern reads as a deliberate statement rather than wallpaper applied everywhere. That surface is a piece of ARCHITECTURE -- a whole wall, an alcove, a chimney breast, a panelled recess or a full run between two real edges -- not a rectangle of pattern floated in the middle of another material like a framed picture. Quieter botanical notes in cushions, artwork, soft furnishings and a subtle secondary treatment tie the room back to it. Balanced with blush-pink surfaces, sage-green accents, ivory finishes, warm natural wood for depth, elegant fixtures and a soft, harmonious atmosphere. The result should feel refined, fresh and professionally composed -- a cohesive botanical interior, not a contemporary room with one floral panel in it.
mandatory: Clearly recognisable floral or botanical motifs must be visible.
The floral treatment must have meaningful presence on an appropriate wall, tile surface or feature area.
The floral pattern is a CONTROLLED feature: ONE dominant floral surface and no more. The remaining walls and large surfaces are plain blush, ivory or sage -- they carry the palette, not the pattern.

That dominant surface must be ARCHITECTURALLY INTEGRATED: it runs the full height and width of a real plane -- a whole wall, an alcove, a chimney breast, a panelled recess, or a full run from corner to corner and skirting to ceiling -- and every edge of it lands on an architectural line. A rectangle of pattern floating in the middle of a different material, framed like a picture or a sample board, is NOT a feature wall and does not satisfy this theme.

Carry the botanical identity into the smaller things as well -- cushions, textiles, artwork, soft furnishings, accessories -- so it is coordinated through the room instead of concentrated in one sheet of wallpaper.

Give the room ONE quieter botanical note besides the dominant surface -- a subtle secondary wall treatment, a soft furnishing, a grouping of botanical artwork -- clearly subordinate to it. One isolated floral element in an otherwise plain contemporary room is not this theme.
Hold the floral motif to one consistent scale, repeating realistically, at a size a real manufacturer would actually print. Do not enlarge it until a few flowers fill a wall.

Blush, sage and ivory should be used coherently where they are compatible with the actual catalog products, with warm natural wood and subtle material texture for depth. No single one of them may take the whole room.

Furniture, cabinetry and furnishings must complement the floral surface rather than compete with it, and must look deliberately coordinated rather than generically arranged, at realistic proportions and in premium materials.

Do not frame the floral surface with a contrasting border, moulding or band of another material -- terracotta, brass, dark trim. A frame is what turns a feature wall back into a panel, and a warm contrasting border pulls the eye off the blush, sage and ivory the theme is built on. Where such a border is an actual selected catalog product, keep it exactly as it is, and keep it narrow and quiet rather than letting it become the edge of a panel.

Large-format grey, stone or neutral surfaces must be BALANCED against warmer ivory, blush and sage ones. Where such a surface is an actual selected catalog product, keep it exactly as it is and warm the room around it -- paint, timber, textiles, soft furnishings -- so the room does not settle into grey.
If the selected catalog tiles are plain, use them honestly and carry the botanical identity on other compatible surfaces or accessories.
Floral detail must be integrated with the architecture, not stuck on it.
avoid: plain pink rooms with no floral elements
a generic modern interior with one potted plant
floral pattern covering most or all of the walls in the room
oversized flower motifs enlarged until a few of them fill a whole surface
a room that reads as overwhelmingly pink, or overwhelmingly green
busy decorative styling with too many ornaments competing for attention
a rectangle of floral pattern floated in the middle of another material, framed like a picture or a sample board
a generic contemporary room with one floral panel in it and nothing else botanical
a terracotta, brass or dark contrasting border framing the floral surface and turning it into a panel
large-format grey or neutral surfaces taking over the room
floral.success: The floral theme is immediately evident from the actual surface treatments and the overall composition, and the pattern is placed selectively rather than spread across every wall, and it is built into the architecture rather than hung on it.
visible: Clearly recognisable floral or botanical motifs are visible.
The floral treatment has meaningful presence on a wall, tile surface or feature area.
The floral pattern is concentrated on one dominant surface, with the other walls plain.
That surface reads as a built part of the room -- a whole wall, alcove or recess -- rather than a framed rectangle set into another material.
A quieter botanical note appears somewhere besides it, in artwork, cushions or soft furnishings.
Warm ivory, blush and sage balance any large grey or neutral surfaces.
No contrasting border or frame runs around the floral surface.
Smaller botanical detail is carried into textiles, cushions, artwork or accessories.
Blush, sage and ivory are all present and balanced, with no single one taking the whole room.
The floral motif is at one consistent scale and repeats realistically.
The furniture and furnishings look deliberately coordinated with the floral scheme.
The floral detail is integrated with the architecture rather than applied on top of it.
counts: A patterned feature wall plus plain walls around it is CORRECT -- that is the controlled distribution this theme asks for, not a missing floral treatment.
Blush is present if you can see it anywhere -- a cushion, a plain wall, a textile. The same for sage and for ivory. None of them has to dominate.
Report the pattern as excessive only when it actually covers most of the walls, or when the motif has been enlarged until a few flowers fill a surface.

INTEGRATED means the floral surface fills a real plane and its edges land on architecture -- a corner, the ceiling, the skirting, a recess. A floral rectangle with another material visible all the way around it is NOT integrated, however large it is.

bedroom: The botanical feature runs the FULL headboard wall -- behind the bed across its whole width, skirting to ceiling, corner to corner -- and the bed stands against it. That wall is the room's focal plane, not a panel hung above the pillows.
A bed with an upholstered or timber headboard in ivory, blush or sage, in realistic proportion to the room.
Bedding layered in warm ivory and blush with sage, and cushions carrying the motif at a smaller scale than the wall.
Side tables and furniture in warm natural timber, soft lamplight, and a quiet rug underfoot.
Botanical artwork or soft furnishings as the quieter second note, in an uncluttered room with few, chosen objects.
living room: A principal sofa in blush pink or sage green, with ivory or warm-cream accent chairs, in realistic proportion to the room.
Refined wooden furniture in warm natural timber, and a coffee table coordinated with it.
Soft decorative cushions and selected botanical artwork, carrying the motif at a smaller scale than the feature surface.
Natural textures and premium fabrics, with balanced curtains or window treatments in a plain or finely patterned cloth.
The feature wall sits behind the seating or the console as the room's focal plane, with the furniture arranged to face it rather than standing in front of it as decoration.
An uncluttered, considered arrangement: the furniture complements the floral surface instead of competing with it, and decorative objects are few and chosen.

tropical.label: Tropical
tropical.palette: Palm green, teal, sand, warm natural wood
tropical.identity: A tropical resort-inspired bathroom with a strong relationship between lush greenery, natural materials and the bathing space. Palm-leaf motifs, tropical botanical patterns, teal accents, sand-toned stone, warm wood and abundant but believable planting. Following the references: large botanical feature surfaces, indoor greenery, natural wood vanities or visually open shower areas. A sophisticated tropical retreat, not a generic bathroom decorated with one plant.
mandatory: Tropical greenery, palm motifs or another unmistakable tropical element must be visible.
Natural materials and the teal/sand relationship must reinforce the theme.
Plants must be plausible for a bathroom and must not obscure the catalog products.
Greenery supports the design; it does not replace proper tile and material planning.
Never fabricate botanical tile patterns as catalog products when none were supplied.
avoid: plain white bathrooms with one plant
British heritage cabinetry as the dominant style
tropical.success: The room feels like a cohesive tropical resort or botanical retreat, with the theme visible throughout the composition.
visible: Tropical greenery, palm motifs or another unmistakable tropical element is visible.
Natural materials and a teal/sand relationship reinforce the theme.
Planting is plausible for a bathroom and does not obscure the tiled surfaces.

geometrical.label: Geometrical
geometrical.identity: A contemporary architectural bathroom defined by strong geometric relationships. Clearly visible geometric tile layouts, angular compositions, hexagonal patterns, repeating forms, structured feature walls or graphic flooring, in the visual language the references demonstrate. A deliberate balance between ivory, graphite and terracotta where the catalog products allow it. The geometry must be intentional, well aligned and part of the architecture.
mandatory: At least one substantial, clearly visible surface must establish the geometric identity.
Patterns must hold consistent alignment, scale, perspective and repetition.
The room must show deliberate geometric composition, not random decorative shapes.
Use the actual catalog tile pattern; invent no additional motif on the product itself.
If the selected tile is plain, carry the geometric identity on other genuine, compatible elements without misrepresenting the product.
avoid: Moroccan ornamentation mistaken for modern geometry
a bathroom with no meaningful geometric feature
geometrical.success: The bathroom reads as a deliberately composed geometric interior, not a generic bathroom with a patterned tile added at random.
visible: At least one substantial, clearly visible surface establishes the geometric identity.
Patterns hold consistent alignment, scale, perspective and repetition.
The room shows deliberate geometric composition rather than random decorative shapes.

metallic.label: Metallic
metallic.identity: A sophisticated contemporary bathroom where metallic finishes and their relationship with reflective or stone surfaces define the design. Pearl-toned stone or tiles, champagne-gold hardware, gunmetal fittings or frames, carefully balanced reflective surfaces and elegant vanity detailing. The identity comes from the coordination of metal finishes, material textures, hardware and lighting -- not from making the whole room gold or silver.
mandatory: Metallic finishes must be clearly visible in fixtures, hardware, frames or other appropriate elements.
Champagne and gunmetal must be balanced deliberately where the references support it.
Pearl-toned surfaces should provide a coherent foundation where they are compatible with the actual catalog tiles.
Metal reflections must be realistic and the different finishes must be distinguishable from one another.
Preserve the actual catalog tile's material appearance.
avoid: generic white marble interiors with no meaningful metallic identity
metallic.success: The complete bathroom feels like a coordinated metallic luxury interior, with believable materials and deliberately selected finishes.
visible: Metallic finishes are clearly visible in fixtures, hardware or frames.
Champagne and gunmetal are balanced deliberately against each other.
Pearl-toned surfaces provide a coherent foundation.
Metal reflections are realistic and the different finishes are distinguishable.

rustic.label: Rustic
rustic.palette: Natural clay, terracotta, ochre, warm wood, earthy stone
rustic.identity: An earthy, handcrafted bathroom: terracotta surfaces, natural clay textures, warm wooden elements, earthy stone and finishes that feel tactile and authentic. Handmade-looking material treatments, subtle surface irregularities, warm natural light and organic composition. Where it fits: terracotta flooring, a natural stone basin, clay-toned walls, rustic timber detail. Grounded, warm and materially honest -- not a polished contemporary bathroom with orange accents.
mandatory: Earthy materials and clay/terracotta tones must have meaningful presence where the catalog products allow it.
Textures should feel natural and tactile rather than artificially distressed.
Wood, stone and clay must work together coherently.
Avoid decorative objects so numerous that they obscure the bathroom design.
Do not turn a smooth catalog tile into a handmade terracotta product by recolouring it or inventing a texture.
avoid: generic white bathrooms with orange accessories
rustic.success: The bathroom feels naturally earthy, warm and handcrafted, and is clearly distinct from the other themes.
visible: Earthy materials and clay or terracotta tones have meaningful presence.
Textures read as natural and tactile rather than artificially distressed.
Wood, stone and clay work together coherently.

moroccan.label: Moroccan
moroccan.palette: Cobalt blue, saffron, warm ivory, terracotta, brass
moroccan.identity: A recognisably Moroccan-inspired bathroom: distinctive zellige-style tilework, intricate mosaic compositions, decorative arches, rich cobalt-blue surfaces, saffron accents and warm brass detail. The interior must communicate Moroccan craftsmanship through its tile arrangements, decorative architecture, material contrasts and overall composition. Traditional hammam architecture or a refined contemporary Moroccan bathroom, according to the supplied references.
mandatory: Moroccan architectural or decorative identity must be clearly visible.
Cobalt-blue or other reference-supported mosaic/zellige surfaces should have meaningful presence where they are compatible with the actual catalog products.
Arches, niches, decorative tile compositions or other unmistakable Moroccan elements should reinforce the style.
Saffron and brass complement the room; they must not overpower it.
Never invent zellige patterns on a selected catalog tile that does not have them.
avoid: arbitrary geometric patterns without Moroccan character
moroccan.success: The room reads as Moroccan-inspired architecture and craftsmanship, not simply a blue bathroom.
visible: Moroccan architectural or decorative identity is clearly visible.
Mosaic or zellige-style surfaces have meaningful presence.
Arches, niches or decorative tile compositions reinforce the style.
Saffron and brass complement the room without overpowering it.

black and white.label: Black & White
black and white.palette: Ivory, ash, charcoal, black and white
black and white.identity: A sophisticated monochromatic bathroom defined by a deliberate balance of ivory, ash, charcoal, black and white. Strong tonal contrast, refined material textures, clean architectural lines and carefully coordinated surfaces. Where the composition calls for it: monochrome patterned tiles, black-and-white flooring, charcoal feature walls, ivory stone, or contrasting vanity and fixture finishes. The whole room must read as an intentional black-and-white interior, not a generic grey bathroom.
mandatory: Black, white, ivory and charcoal must create a clear, intentional monochromatic composition.
Contrast must be carried across several elements -- tiles, walls, flooring, vanity or fixtures.
Preserve the actual selected catalog tiles' original colours, patterns and textures.
Ash and charcoal are supporting tones; the room must not flatten into grey.
Keep visual balance, realistic materials and a coherent overall composition.
avoid: a plain white bathroom with no meaningful contrast
generic grey-on-grey interiors with no distinctive monochromatic identity
black and white.success: The complete bathroom is immediately recognisable as a deliberately designed black-and-white interior, through its contrast, material choices, tile placement and overall composition.
visible: Black, white, ivory and charcoal form a clear, intentional monochromatic composition.
Contrast is carried across several elements -- tiles, walls, flooring, vanity or fixtures.
The room has real contrast rather than flattening into grey.
